I found why CI is failing, but not the root cause. A new test added in #15 is flaky on CI's x64 runners. Your code changes in that PR aren't what fails.

**What fails:** `tests/native-stderr.test.ts`, at `expect(result.status).toBe(0)` (lines 35 and 42). Since #15 merged, every `main` run has failed on this test, sometimes on one Node version and sometimes on both. The PR's own CI run passed on both.

**What it tells us:** `status` is `null`, which means the child Node process was killed by a signal rather than exiting with an error code. It dies after about 1.1 s, so it isn't the 60 s timeout.

The test that sets `PI_PII_REDACT_NATIVE_LOGS=1` also crashes. In that mode `withSilencedNativeStderr` skips libc and does nothing, so the file-descriptor redirect from #15 isn't the cause. The child crashes while it runs or shuts down the model.

**Likely cause (not confirmed):** the child loads the model, runs it, calls `dispose()` and exits. On Linux the model's native core calls back into Node from its own threads for license checks. Its source carries a warning that these koffi callbacks can "hang or crash it at exit" (`node_modules/@desert-ant-labs/core/src/native.js:84`). A crash that only happens sometimes, during that teardown, fits a race in the native library. No earlier test checks how a model process exits, which explains why this is the first time it shows up.

**Why I couldn't confirm it here:** this machine is aarch64 and CI is x64. I ran the exact child script 80 times locally and it exited cleanly every time. Docker isn't available to emulate x64. The test also doesn't print the signal or the child's stderr when it fails, so the CI logs don't show what killed it.

**Separate, harmless:** the `changeset-release/main` "Version Packages" runs fail with no jobs ("workflow file issue"). The same happened before #13 and `main` still went green, so it's unrelated.

**Suggested next steps:**
1. Make the test's failure message include `result.signal` and `result.stderr`, and push that to a branch so CI shows which signal kills the child.
2. Then fix it based on what that shows. The most likely fix is to have the test check the stderr content and `stderr-restored` but not a clean exit code after `dispose()`. Another option is to have the child exit before native teardown. If the crash is in the library itself, report it upstream to `@desert-ant-labs`.

# Masker Mini (v3)

**Masker-mini** is the on-device sibling of
[**masker**](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker). It is a 6-layer
distilled PII detector for **23 European languages** that fits in **18 MB**
(4-bit Core ML) or **22 MB** (4-bit ONNX).

It runs fully offline, so no PII leaves the device.

| artifact                            | format                    | size      | token agreement vs fp32 | strict F1 |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------- | ----------------------- | --------- |
| `model.safetensors`                 | PyTorch fp16              | 71 MB     | —                       | 0.975     |
| `onnx/model_fp16.onnx`              | ONNX fp16 (portable)      | 71 MB     | 100%                    | 0.975     |
| `onnx/model_int4.onnx`              | ONNX 4-bit (ONNX Runtime) | **22 MB** | 99.95%                  | 0.975     |
| `coreml/masker_mini_4bit.mlpackage` | Core ML 4-bit (Apple NE)  | **18 MB** | 99.93%                  | 0.974     |

Per-artifact columns are measured on a 2,000-document openpii validation sample.

### What's new in v3

- **Much better on real text.** On out-of-distribution person names (real court
  judgments and Dutch news), names F1 goes from **0.774 → 0.865**. Leak recall
  goes from 0.868 → 0.922. It beats `nationaldesignstudio/rampart` (0.690) and
  `desert-ant-labs/redact` (0.626) on every metric we measure.
- **Far fewer false names in Dutch.** On CoNLL-2002 NL, the share of other named
  entities (companies, places) wrongly tagged as persons drops from **16.4% →
  7.0%**.
- **One change caused it: the student now starts from pretrained weights.** v2's
  student started from random weights, so everything it knew about language came
  from the distillation data. v3 starts from the bottom six layers of
  [Multilingual-MiniLM](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Multilingual-MiniLM-L12-H384),
  moved onto masker's 64K tokenizer. The teacher, the data and the recipe are
  otherwise identical to v2.
- **Drop-in replacement for v2.** The architecture, `config.json`, label map,
  tokenizer files (byte-identical), inputs and outputs are all the same. You only
  swap the weights. v2 is kept under the
  [`v2` tag](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker-mini/tree/v2).

## Model type & training
## Usage

For a plain PyTorch / Transformers quick start, the snippet on the
[masker](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker) card runs unchanged. Just
point it at `divergentlabs/masker-mini`.

This repo exists mainly for the two on-device builds:

**ONNX Runtime** (portable for Android, iOS, web, server)

```python
import onnxruntime as ort, numpy as np
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

repo = "divergentlabs/masker-mini"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(repo)
sess = ort.InferenceSession(hf_hub_download(repo, "onnx/model_fp16.onnx"))
text = "Sanne de Groot woont in Utrecht."
feed = {k: v.astype(np.int64) for k, v in tok(text, return_tensors="np").items()}
logits = sess.run(None, feed)[0]        # [1, seq_len, 49] BIOES logits -> argmax + decode
```

For the smallest portable build, swap in `onnx/model_int4.onnx` (22 MB, 4-bit).
It has the same inputs and outputs and needs ONNX Runtime ≥ 1.18.

**Swift (iOS / macOS):** [**swift-masker**](https://github.com/divergentlabsxyz/swift-masker)
is a Swift package that wraps the Core ML build with tokenization, the
BIOES→span decode, the structured-PII rules layer, and reversible masking. It
bundles its own copy of the model. v3 uses the same tokenizer and interface as
v2, so the bundled model can be swapped without code changes.

```swift
// .package(url: "https://github.com/divergentlabsxyz/swift-masker.git", from: "0.1.0")
let masker = try await Masker()
let masked = try await masker.mask(userText)   // "[EMAIL_1] lives in [CITY_1]"
let final  = masker.unmask(reply, with: masked.session)
```

To use the **Core ML** model directly, add
`coreml/masker_mini_4bit.mlpackage` to an Xcode target. Its inputs are
`input_ids`, `attention_mask` and `token_type_ids` (`Int32`, fixed length 256),
and its output is `logits` (`[1, 256, 49]`, fp16). Tokenize with this repo's
`spm.model` / `tokenizer.json`.

## Limitations & biases

- **Some Dutch over-redaction remains.** On CoNLL-2002 NL, 7.0% of the other
  named entities are still tagged as persons, against 2.7% for the teacher. Brand
  names built from a person's name are the typical case: "Albert Heijn" (a
  supermarket chain) is tagged as a person. For Dutch documents where
  over-redaction matters, use [masker](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker).
- **Dutch _tussenvoegsel_ surnames may be mistyped on short inputs.** v2 sometimes
  typed the surname of "Sanne de Groot" or "Pieter van den Berg" as
  `STREET_NAME` or `CITY`. We did not reproduce this with v3, but have not ruled
  it out. When it happens, the characters are still redacted; only the
  placeholder type is wrong.
- **This is a compressed model.** It trails the full-size masker (v2) by about
  0.9 points strict F1 in-distribution and by 7.3 points names F1 on real text. The
  loss lands almost entirely on `GIVEN_NAME` / `SURNAME`. Structured types (email,

  Measure on your own text, and design for residual leakage rather than assuming

I think it's worth a trial, but I wouldn't switch straight over. Its main advantages: it would drop the closed native library that segfaults on exit, it's Apache-2.0, and it claims better name detection. The catch is that it covers about half the PII types we redact today, and we'd have to build the runtime pieces that `@desert-ant-labs/redact` currently gives us.

**What it improves**
- **It would drop the crash we just found.** The segfault, the use of koffi to call native code, and the license-verifier callback all come from `@desert-ant-labs`. The current core also has a license endpoint and telemetry hooks. masker-mini is Apache-2.0 open weights run through ONNX Runtime, with nothing calling home.
- **Names.** Their card claims a person-name F1 of 0.865 versus 0.626 for `desert-ant-labs/redact` on real text (English court judgments and Dutch news). The authors measured that themselves and nobody has verified it, but names are where false negatives hurt us most.
- **Languages and portability:** it covers 23 European languages, and the ONNX file runs on Node, the web and mobile.

**What we'd lose**
- **Label coverage.** It has 12 types: `GIVEN_NAME`, `SURNAME`, `STREET_NAME`, `BUILDING_NUMBER`, `CITY`, `ZIP_CODE`, `EMAIL`, `PHONE`, `CREDIT_CARD`, `GOVERNMENT_ID`, `DATE` and `AGE`. Our rules use 22. These would have no model behind them:
  - `SECONDARY_ADDRESS`, `STATE`, `BANK_ACCOUNT`, `ROUTING_NUMBER`, `URL`
  - `PASSPORT`, `DRIVERS_LICENSE`, `TAX_ID`, `SSN`, `IMEI`, `ORG`

  Only email, IP address and generic API keys have regex rules today, so most of these would need new regex rules or would simply stop being redacted. It also adds `DATE`, which could over-redact dates in timestamps, git logs and changelogs, which is a lot of what a coding agent reads. I'd ship `DATE` disabled by default.
- **We'd have to build what the current SDK does for us:**
  - `onnxruntime-node`, which is another native dependency, though a mainstream and well-maintained one.
  - A JavaScript tokenizer for its SentencePiece `tokenizer.json`.
  - Decoding its BIOES tags into character spans.
  - Softmax confidence scores for `minimumConfidence`.
  - Splitting inputs longer than 512 tokens into overlapping windows, since tool output is often long.

  `@huggingface/transformers` could handle the tokenizer and runtime, but its token-classification pipeline doesn't decode BIOES tags properly, so we'd write that part ourselves.

**fp16 vs int4:** I'd lean towards `model_int4.onnx` (22 MB, 99.95% agreement with full precision) rather than fp16 (71 MB). On CPU, ONNX Runtime has optimised kernels for the 4-bit format, while fp16 often gets converted back to fp32 and may not be faster. The int4 file is also about the size of today's model (24 MB cached). Their card shows the same 0.975 F1 for both.

**What I'd suggest:** a time-boxed trial behind a small backend interface in `RedactorService`, keeping the current model as the default. We'd run the existing e2e tiers against both backends, comparing what leaks, false positives on code and logs, latency and memory. If the trial wins, switching becomes a config change and we add regex rules for the lost types. If it loses, we've only spent the trial.

# Masker (v2)

**masker** is a multilingual token classifier for personally identifiable
information (PII) in **23 European languages**. It is the neural half of a
two-part redaction system. This model tags _contextual_ PII: names, addresses,
ages and dates.

A separate, dependency-free rules layer handles _structured_ PII (IBANs, cards,
national IDs) with real checksum validation. Where both fire on the same span,
the checksum-validated rule wins. Everywhere else, the model decides. This
repository is the neural half and the **full-accuracy reference model** of the
family.

📱 Need something small enough to run on a phone or in a web browser? See
[**masker-mini**](https://huggingface.co/divergentlabs/masker-mini), a 6-layer
[`microsoft/mdeberta-v3-base`](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/mdeberta-v3-base)
with **boundary-first BIOES supervision**. It was trained for 1 epoch on 1.44M
rows: name-form-augmented
[`ai4privacy/pii-masking-openpii-1m`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4privacy/pii-masking-openpii-1m)
plus the real-text corpora. In the real text, person spans come from the gold
annotations (split into given name and surname by masker v1, or by rule), and the other
PII types are pseudo-labelled by masker v1.

The head predicts **12 entity types** (48 BIOES labels + `O`):

`GIVEN_NAME`, `SURNAME`, `CITY`, `STREET_NAME`, `BUILDING_NUMBER`, `ZIP_CODE`,
`PHONE`, `EMAIL`, `CREDIT_CARD`, `DATE`, `AGE`, `GOVERNMENT_ID`.

`GOVERNMENT_ID` covers passport, national-ID, SSN, tax and driver-license
numbers; the rules layer tells them apart by checksum and format. Other
structured types (IBAN, IP, URL, etc.) are owned entirely by the rules layer and
are not part of this head.

## Usage

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForTokenClassification
import torch

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("divergentlabs/masker")
model = AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained("divergentlabs/masker").eval()

text = "Kundin Beatrix Möller, geb. 04.07.1979, Rosenweg 8, 50667 Köln."
enc = tok(text, return_tensors="pt", return_offsets_mapping=True)
offsets = enc.pop("offset_mapping")[0]
with torch.no_grad():
    labels = model(**enc).logits.argmax(-1)[0]
for (a, b), lab in zip(offsets.tolist(), labels.tolist()):
    if b > a and model.config.id2label[lab] != "O":
        print(text[a:b].strip(), "->", model.config.id2label[lab])
```

The raw output is per-token BIOES labels. The companion `mask` package turns
them into character spans and merges them with the rules layer. The tokenizer's
offsets include the leading space of word-initial pieces, so trim whitespace
from span edges.

content.text:
The masker-mini backend is working on branch `t3/masker-mini-backend` and I've run the comparison. My recommendation is not to switch to it as-is. It's 3–4× faster and better on European names and addresses. But it misses or mislabels much of the structured PII (phones, cards, SSNs, IBANs) that the current model catches, and that's the kind of leak this extension exists to prevent.

Everything is uncommitted on the branch. It runs only when you set `PI_PII_REDACT_BACKEND=masker-mini`, so default behaviour doesn't change, and the two new packages are dev dependencies only.

**Comparison** (my own 34-text corpus, run through the full redaction pipeline on this ARM machine; too small to settle the question, but the patterns are clear):

| | current model | masker-mini int4 | masker-mini fp16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Median time per text | 78 ms | **26 ms** | 41 ms |
| 2.9k-char tool output | 3.1 s | **0.8 s** | 1.2 s |
| Memory (RSS) | 189 MB | 267 MB | 307 MB |
| Load time | 0.4 s | 0.4 s | 0.7 s |

- **European text (masker-mini better):** it caught everything in a German sentence (name, street, house number, zip, city) where the current model caught nothing. It also caught "Via Roma 22" in Italian and split Dutch names into given name and surname properly.
- **Other names (masker-mini worse):** it missed "Wei Zhang", "Raghunathan" and "Fernández García", which the current model caught. That fits its European-only training data.
- **Structured PII (masker-mini much worse):**
  - **Missed completely:** `+31 6 1234 5678`, the SSN `123-45-6789`, and the IBAN.
  - **Labelled as phone numbers:** both credit cards. One was split so that `1111` stayed in plain text.
  - **Cut short:** one phone number, leaving `6543` visible.
- **False positives on code and logs:** about the same. The only extra one was `issue #1284` tagged as a building number.
- **fp16 vs int4:** same detections, but fp16 is slower and uses more memory. int4 is the better variant.
- **Existing test suite on masker-mini:** 11 of about 400 tests fail. Ten are card and phone cases. The eleventh is a quirk of the test setup that counts model loads, not a detection failure. The default suite still passes (396 passed, 13 skipped), and the new masker-mini tests pass on both variants.

**Review notes:**
- **Fixed:** `MaskerMini` used constructor syntax that Node can't load when running the package's TypeScript source directly. It worked under the tests but failed outside them. I rewrote it with plain fields; it was the only file in `src/` with that syntax.
- **Not fixed:** detected spans sometimes include trailing punctuation (`5,`).

**Your options:**
1. **Stop here** and keep the current model. The branch stays around as a reference.
2. **Switch to masker-mini fully.** This is the design its authors intended: the model handles names, addresses, dates and ages, and checksum-validated regex rules handle cards, IBANs, SSNs and phones. It would remove the native library that segfaults, but it's a sizeable project and needs a much bigger labelled test set first.
3. **Run both:** masker-mini for names and addresses, the current model for structured PII. That combines their strengths but keeps the segfaulting library, plus extra load time and memory.

I'd lean towards option 2 if dropping the native library matters to you, otherwise option 1. Which way do you want to go, and should I commit and push this branch as a draft PR in the meantime?
go for 2

Option 2 it is. That's a multi-part project, so I'll settle the two open design questions first. One is which ONNX runtime to ship, since `onnxruntime-node` bundles binaries for every platform (about 300 MB installed). The other is what the reference rules layer covers. I'll fetch the Swift rules code and benchmark the WebAssembly runtime as a lighter alternative.

I'd add it, with some guardrails, as a follow-up PR after the masker-mini switch rather than inside it. The case for it: our current secret detection is one regex that only knows OpenAI-style `sk-…`, GitHub, GitLab and AWS key IDs. This package brings 1,044 rules (gitleaks plus kingfisher), and it produced no false positives on my test text.

**What I measured:**
- **Coverage:** with realistic keys it caught Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe, AWS key pairs, Hugging Face, Slack, SendGrid, Google, GitLab, GitHub PATs, JWTs, PEM private keys, `postgres://user:pass@` URLs and `password = "…"` assignments. It missed `npm_…` tokens and the AWS documentation example key `AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE`, which it deliberately ignores. Our existing regex rule catches the AWS one, so we'd keep that rule as a fallback.
- **False positives:** none on the 370-case eval corpus, including all 125 developer texts with no PII (hashes, commit SHAs, `sha512-` integrity strings, UUIDs, base64 images, `process.env.API_KEY`). All 6 labelled API keys there were found except that AWS example key.
- **Speed:** each call costs a fixed ~24 ms, even for a 50-character string. It can't be avoided by passing the ruleset in, and calls don't run in parallel. That's more than our whole pipeline today (14 ms median). A cheap pre-check skipped the scanner for 320 of 370 corpus texts without missing any key in this test. It only calls the scanner when the text contains something key-shaped: a 20+ character token, `-----BEGIN`, a `user:pass@` URL, or a `password=`/`token:`-style assignment.
- **Package:** MIT licensed, about 30k downloads a week, but young (first release April 2026). It's another native addon (Rust via N-API) shipped as a 2.8 MB package per platform, much lighter than ONNX Runtime. It needs Node ^22.14 or ≥24.10.

**Guardrails it would need:**
- **No network:** it can check whether a found key is live by sending it to the provider, or by connecting to a database URL it found. That's off by default, but we'd hard-code `validate: false` and an empty allowed-hosts list so a secret can never leave the machine that way.
- **Span selection:** some rules return huge spans. `curl-auth-header` reported the whole `curl …` command as the secret. We'd take the narrowest finding where findings overlap, and skip multi-word spans except for private-key blocks.
- **Labels and precedence:** findings would get a `SECRET` token and run before the PII rules, so a phone or IBAN rule can't grab digits out of a key. Restore still works: if the model writes `[SECRET_1#…]` in a tool call, the real key goes into the actual command, so the agent can use credentials without ever seeing them.
- **Failing safe:** if the native binding can't load on some platform, we'd warn once and fall back to the existing regex rule rather than failing redaction.
- **Process exit:** given the earlier segfault, I'd add the scanner to the clean-exit test alongside ONNX Runtime.
